back: An identity anything can assume temporarily (EC2, Lambda, another account) via STS for short-lived credentials -- the recommended alternative to long-term access keys.
Always wins over any Allow in IAM policy evaluation, no matter how many policies grant access or which was attached most recently.
Stateful, instance/ENI-level virtual firewall. Allow-only rules; allowing inbound automatically allows the matching outbound response.
Stateless, subnet-level firewall. Supports both Allow and Deny rules, evaluated in numbered order.
Directly-attached, ephemeral EC2 disk. Fast and often free, but wiped on stop/termination -- scratch data only.
Elastic Block Store -- durable, network-attached disk that persists independently of the instance lifecycle (unless delete-on-termination is set).
Once enabled, keeps every version of an object. Can be suspended later, but never fully turned back off.
Automatically transitions objects between storage classes (or expires them) as they age, without manual intervention.
Not a distinct resource type -- just a subnet whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway.
Sits in a public subnet; lets private-subnet resources reach the internet outbound without being reachable from it. Scoped to one AZ.
Not transitive. If A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B -- use a Transit Gateway for many-VPC connectivity.
Lets resources reach AWS services without the public internet or a NAT Gateway. Gateway endpoints (free, S3/DynamoDB) vs Interface endpoints (billed, PrivateLink).
ALB = Layer 7, HTTP-aware, path/host routing. NLB = Layer 4, raw TCP/UDP, lowest latency, static IP per AZ.
Protects against a data-center-level failure within one region. The default resilience target for most workloads.
Protects against a whole-region failure, at much higher cost/complexity. A deliberate tradeoff, not a default best practice.
Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, Sustainability -- six total.
The simplest Auto Scaling Group policy: declare a target metric value (e.g. 50% avg CPU) and AWS adjusts capacity to hold it there.
Failover, weighted, latency-based, and geolocation -- all driven by health checks, entirely at the DNS layer.
Global -- unlike EC2, VPC, and EBS, which are all regional.
Scaled score of 720 out of 1000 -- NOT literally 72% of raw questions, since AWS scales per-question difficulty.
